problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###

**a. Verdict:**  
I have successfully solved the problem. The minimum number of tiles required is  

\[
\boxed{}.
\]

**b. Method Sketch:**  

1. **Permutation model.**  
   The uncovered squares form a permutation matrix: there is a permutation \(p\) of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\) (\(n=2025\)) such that the uncovered square in row \(i\) lies in column \(p(i)\).  
   For each column \(j\) let \(r_j:=p^{-1}(j)\) be the row of its uncovered square.

2. **Two monotone regions.**  
   Define  
   \[
   A=\{(i,j)\mid i<r_j\}\qquad\text{(cells strictly **above** the hole of their column)},
   \]
   \[
   B=\{(i,j)\mid i>r_j\}\qquad\text{(cells strictly **below** the hole of their column)} .
   \]
   Every unit square of the board belongs either to \(A\) or to \(B\); the uncovered squares themselves are excluded.  
   Consequently every tile is contained entirely in \(A\) or entirely in \(B\) for each column it meets.  
   The shapes of \(A\) and \(B\) are the two stair‑case Young diagrams of shape \((n-1,n-2,\dots ,1)\).

3. **A set of mutually incompatible cells.**  
   For each row \(i\) consider the cells that are **adjacent horizontally** to the uncovered square:
   \[
   L_i=
   \begin{cases}
   (i,p(i)-1), & p(i)>1,\\[2pt]
   \text{none}, & p(i)=1,
   \end{cases}
   \qquad
   R_i=
   \begin{cases}
   (i,p(i)+1), & p(i)<n,\\[2pt]
   \text{none}, & p(i)=n .
   \end{cases}
   \]
   Let  
   \[
   \mathcal C:=\bigl\{L_i\mid p(i)>1\bigr\}\cup\bigl\{R_i\mid p(i)<n\bigr\}.
   \]
   Because the first column and the last column each contain exactly one uncovered square, \(|\mathcal C|=2n-2\).

   **Lemma 1.** *No axis‑aligned rectangle can contain two distinct cells of \(\mathcal C\).*  

   *Proof.*  
   Suppose a rectangle \(R\) contains two distinct cells of \(\mathcal C\).  
   There are three possibilities.

   *Both are left‑adjacent cells:* \(X=(i,p(i)-1)\) and \(Y=(k,p(k)-1)\) with \(i<k\).  
   Since \(p\) is a permutation, either \(p(i)<p(k)\) or \(p(i)>p(k)\).  
   If \(p(i)<p(k)\) then the column \(p(i)\) lies strictly between the columns \(p(i)-1\) and \(p(k)-1\) of \(R\); the row \(i\) lies between the rows of \(R\).  
   Hence the hole \((i,p(i))\) belongs to \(R\), contradicting the rule that tiles may not cover uncovered squares.  
   The case \(p(i)>p(k)\) is symmetric.  

   *Both are right‑adjacent cells:* the argument is identical, using the columns \(p(i)+1\) and \(p(k)+1\).

   *One left‑adjacent and one right‑adjacent:* say \(X=(i,p(i)-1)\) and \(Y=(k,p(k)+1)\) with \(i\le k\).  
   If \(p(i)\le p(k)\) then column \(p(i)\) lies between the columns of \(R\); together with row \(i\) this forces the hole \((i,p(i))\) to be inside \(R\).  
   If \(p(i)>p(k)\) then column \(p(k)+1\) lies between the columns of \(R\) and row \(k\) forces the hole \((k,p(k))\) to be inside \(R\).  
   In every sub‑case a hole is covered, which is impossible. ∎  

   Consequently each rectangle can cover **at most one** cell of \(\mathcal C\).  

   Since \(|\mathcal C|=2n-2\), any tiling of the whole board needs at least \(2n-2\) rectangles.

4. **Construction attaining the bound.**  
   For each column \(j\) (with hole at row \(r_j\)) place  

   * a vertical tile covering rows \(1,\dots ,r_j-1\) (if \(r_j>1\)), and  
   * a vertical tile covering rows \(r_j+1,\dots ,n\) (if \(r_j<n\)).  

   These tiles are disjoint because they lie in distinct columns, and together they cover every square except the uncovered ones.  
   The total number of tiles is  

   \[
   \sum_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(\mathbf 1_{\,r_j>1}+\mathbf 1_{\,r_j<n}\bigr)
   =2n-\bigl(\#\{j\mid r_j=1\}+\#\{j\mid r_j=n\}\bigr)
   =2n-2,
   \]
   because exactly one column contains the hole in row 1 and exactly one column contains the hole in row \(n\).

5. **Conclusion.**  
   The lower bound \(2n-2\) and the explicit construction both give the same number, so the minimum possible number of tiles is \(2n-2\).  
   For \(n=2025\),

   \[
   2\cdot2025-2 = 4048 .
   \]

   Hence the answer is  

   \[
   \boxed{4048}.
   \]

---

### Detailed Solution ###

Let \(n=2025\).  Index the rows by \(R_1,\dots ,R_n\) and the columns by \(C_1,\dots ,C_n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 1.  The uncovered squares form a permutation matrix  

Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, there exists a permutation \(p\) of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\) such that the uncovered square in row \(i\) lies at column \(p(i)\).  
Equivalently, for each column \(j\) there is a unique row  

\[
r_j:=p^{-1}(j)
\]

containing the uncovered square of that column.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.  Decomposition into two monotone regions  

Define  

\[
A:=\{(i,j)\mid i<r_j\},\qquad   
B:=\{(i,j)\mid i>r_j\}.
\]

Every unit square of the board belongs either to \(A\) or to \(B\); the uncovered squares themselves are excluded.

*Claim.*  A rectangular tile cannot contain squares from both \(A\) and \(B\) belonging to the same column.  
Indeed, if a tile intersected column \(j\) in rows both \(\le r_j-1\) and \(\ge r_j+1\), then its row interval would contain \(r_j\) and the tile would cover the uncovered square \((r_j,j)\), which is forbidden.  
Hence for each column a tile is either completely **above** the hole (entirely in \(A\)) or completely **below** the hole (entirely in \(B\)).

The shape of \(A\) is the Young diagram with row lengths \(n-1,n-2,\dots ,1,0\); the shape of \(B\) is its vertical reflection, also with row lengths \(0,1,2,\dots ,n-1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.  A set of mutually incompatible cells  

For every row \(i\) consider the cells that are horizontally adjacent to the uncovered square:

\[
L_i=
\begin{cases}
(i,p(i)-1), & p(i)>1,\\
\text{none}, & p(i)=1,
\end{cases}
\qquad
R_i=
\begin{cases}
(i,p(i)+1), & p(i)<n,\\
\text{none}, & p(i)=n .
\end{cases}
\]

Let  

\[
\mathcal C:=\{L_i\mid p(i)>1\}\cup\{R_i\mid p(i)<n\}.
\]

Because exactly one uncovered square lies in column 1 and exactly one lies in column \(n\), the first row contributes no left‑adjacent cell and the last row contributes no right‑adjacent cell; all other rows contribute two cells.  Hence  

\[
|\mathcal C| = 2n-2 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Lemma 1  
*No axis‑aligned rectangle can contain two distinct cells of \(\mathcal C\).*

*Proof.*  
Assume a rectangle \(R\) contains two distinct cells of \(\mathcal C\).  
Three cases are possible.

1. **Both cells are left‑adjacent.**  
   Let \(X=(i,p(i)-1)\) and \(Y=(k,p(k)-1)\) with \(i<k\).  
   Since \(p\) is a permutation, either \(p(i)<p(k)\) or \(p(i)>p(k)\).

   *If \(p(i)<p(k)\):* the column \(p(i)\) lies strictly between the columns \(p(i)-1\) and \(p(k)-1\) of \(R\); the row \(i\) lies between the rows of \(R\).  
   Consequently the hole \((i,p(i))\) belongs to \(R\), contradicting the rule that tiles may not cover uncovered squares.

   *If \(p(i)>p(k)\):* the symmetric argument uses column \(p(k)\) and yields the same contradiction.

2. **Both cells are right‑adjacent.**  
   The argument is identical, replacing each “\(-1\)” by “\(+1\)”.

3. **One left‑adjacent and one right‑adjacent.**  
   Suppose \(X=(i,p(i)-1)\) and \(Y=(k,p(k)+1)\) with \(i\le k\).  

   If \(p(i)\le p(k)\), then column \(p(i)\) lies between the columns of \(R\); together with row \(i\) this forces the hole \((i,p(i))\) to be inside \(R\).  
   If \(p(i)>p(k)\), then column \(p(k)+1\) lies between the columns of \(R\) and row \(k\) forces the hole \((k,p(k))\) to be inside \(R\).  

   In either sub‑case a hole is covered, which is impossible.

Thus any rectangle can contain at most one element of \(\mathcal C\). ∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.  Lower bound on the number of tiles  

Since each tile is a rectangle and the tiles are pairwise disjoint, Lemma 1 implies that each tile can cover at most one cell of \(\mathcal C\).  
Because \(|\mathcal C|=2n-2\), any tiling of the board must use at least \(2n-2\) tiles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.  Construction attaining the bound  

For each column \(j\) (hole at row \(r_j\)) place  

* a vertical tile covering rows \(1,2,\dots ,r_j-1\) if \(r_j>1\);  
* a vertical tile covering rows \(r_j+1,r_j+2,\dots ,n\) if \(r_j<n\).

These tiles lie in distinct columns, so they do not overlap, and together they cover every square except the uncovered ones.  

The total number of tiles is  

\[
\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(\mathbf 1_{\,r_j>1}+\mathbf 1_{\,r_j<n}\bigr)
=2n-\bigl(\#\{j\mid r_j=1\}+\#\{j\mid r_j=n\}\bigr)
=2n-2,
\]

because exactly one column contains the hole in row 1 and exactly one column contains the hole in row \(n\).

Thus a tiling with \(2n-2\) tiles exists.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 6.  Conclusion  

The lower bound \(2n-2\) and the explicit construction both give the same number, so the minimum possible number of tiles is \(2n-2\).  
For the given board with \(n=2025\),

\[
2\cdot2025-2 = 4048 .
\]

Hence the answer is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]
